Bed Bug Control
Bed bugs are notoriously difficult to eradicate due to their ability to hide in crevices and fold
areas of furniture. The following methodology outlines a recommended approach using
heat, steam, and chemical treatments.
Note: For client situations, a licensed pest control contractor should always be consulted.
Step-by-Step Procedure
1. Mattress and Upholstery Treatment
• Use hot water extraction (≥145°F / 63°C) or live steam to clean mattresses,
box springs, and all upholstered furniture.
• Ensure thorough treatment of folds, seams, and crevices, as these are
common hiding spots for bed bugs.
2. Carpet Extraction
• Extract carpets using high-temperature water (≥145°F / 63°C).
• Where feasible, add a quaternary disinfectant to the solution for added
efficacy.
3. Baseboard Treatment
• Spray insecticide along baseboards at the perimeter of the room.
• Repeat this process approximately every 20 days, as bed bugs can hide in
small gaps and crevices.
4. Furniture Perimeter Treatment
• Spray around the base of beds and upholstered furniture on carpeted areas
to prevent bed bug migration.
5. Drying Time
• Allow treated surfaces to dry for 6–8 hours before reoccupation or further
cleaning.
6. Upholstery Deodorizer Application
• Apply CA 570 undiluted to all upholstered surfaces.
• This deodorizer also discourages bed bug reproduction in treated areas.

Important Notes
• Multiple methods exist for bed bug eradication; this procedure reﬂects one
effective approach.
• Bed bugs are crevice-dwelling insects and may require repeated treatments.
• Identiﬁcation and professional guidance are recommended when clients are
uncertain about infestation.

Carpet Spotting
The goal of carpet spotting is to remove foreign materials from ﬁbers without causing
damage. Successful spot removal requires understanding both the type of ﬁber and the
nature of the stain. In some cases, the stain’s origin is unknown, requiring careful
observation, touch, and even smell to identify or categorize the spot.
Identifying Stains
1. Ask
When possible, ask the customer or employees if they know the origin of the stain. This is
often the fastest way to identify it.
2. Sight
• Shape: Round, square, or geometric spots are usually transferred from objects
(e.g., chair legs), while irregular shapes often indicate spills. Spots in a line may
indicate dripping from a moving object.
• Appearance: Shiny spots often indicate hardened oils (paint, varnish, nail
polish), while dull spots may be food related. Lighter spots can indicate dye loss.
• Location: Consider the surrounding area for clues—e.g., a spot near a soda
machine is likely a beverage spill.
• Depth: Examine whether the stain is only on the yarn surface or has penetrated
deeper, which may indicate wicking from prior cleaning.
3. Touch
Learn to recognize the texture of different stains: tacky, waxy, hard, soft, oily, dry, or wet.
Familiarity with these textures aids future identiﬁcation.
4. Smell
Odor can be a strong indicator of stain type. Your experience and sensitivity will determine
how effective smell helps in identiﬁcation.
5. pH Consideration
If a stain does not respond to dry solvents, it may be water-soluble. In these cases, the pH
of the cleaning solution may play a role in removal.

General Rules for Spot & Stain Removal
1. Assess all available information and plan the approach.
2. Select appropriate chemical agents.
3. Test the agent on a small, inconspicuous area to ensure it does not damage
ﬁbers or alter colors.
4. Remove excess, built-up, or crusted material with a spatula or similar tool.
5. Apply the cleaning agent sparingly—avoid over-wetting.
6. Blot gently; do not scrub or brush harshly, as this can fuzz or damage ﬁbers.
7. Work from the edge of the stain toward the center to prevent rings.
8. Allow sufficient time (2–5 minutes) for the chemical to work.
9. Remove excess chemical by blotting and lightly ﬂush with water. If additional
agents are required, repeat the steps.
Tip: When using steam or hot water extraction, spot after cleaning. Pre-spotting is
recommended for other cleaning methods.
Practical Guidelines for Stain Removal
• Immediate Action: Blot liquid stains immediately with a soft, white, absorbent
towel.
• Never Scrub: Scrubbing can embed stains into ﬁbers and damage the carpet.
• Test First: Always pre-test any cleaning agent in an inconspicuous area for color-
fastness. Apply a small amount to each color, cover with a white towel for ~30
seconds, and check for color transfer or damage.
• Application: Apply the spot remover from the edges toward the center using a
stainless-steel spoon or similar tool.
• Sequential Cleaning: If multiple cleaning agents are needed, continue with the
ﬁrst agent until no further improvement occurs, then move on to the next.
• Rinsing: After the stain is removed, rinse the area with water and blot dry.
Residual chemicals can attract soil and damage the carpet. Use heavy objects
on towels to blot excess water.
• Avoid Over-Wetting: Excess water can damage carpet backing or ﬁbers.

Chemical Dispensing
During times of product shortages or supplier changes, many facilities have had to switch
cleaning brands or formulations to maintain consistent hygiene standards. While cleaning
chemicals are essential for health and sanitation, they also pose risks when mixed or
handled improperly.
According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), between January and
March of 2020, poison control centers received 45,550 exposure calls related to cleaners
and disinfectants — a 20.4% increase from the same period in 2019. This underscores the
importance of safe and accurate chemical management in every cleaning program.
The Role of Chemical Dispensing Systems
Chemical dispensers are engineered to make cleaning safer, simpler, and more consistent.
Though not new technology, they have become increasingly valuable in modern cleaning
programs due to their precision and user safety.
These systems — available in wall-mounted or portable formats — are designed to hold
one or more concentrated chemicals. They automatically dilute and dispense the correct
ratio of cleaning solution with water, eliminating the need for manual measuring or mixing.
How Chemical Dispensers Work
A chemical dispenser operates on a simple principle:
It draws a controlled amount of concentrated chemical and blends it with water at a
precise dilution ratio, producing a ready-to-use solution.
Step-by-step process:
1. The user connects the dispenser to a clean water source.
2. The system draws chemical concentrate through a calibrated injector.
3. Water pressure passes through the unit, mixing the chemical and water at the
correct ratio.
4. The diluted solution is released directly into a spray bottle, mop bucket, or auto
scrubber tank — ready for safe use.
This process ensures consistent cleaning results, eliminates waste, and reduces the risk of
human error or chemical exposure.

Advantages of Using Chemical Dispensers
• Safety: Prevents contact with concentrated chemicals and minimizes risk of
spills or splashes.
• Accuracy: Ensures correct dilution every time, maximizing cleaning
performance.
• Cost Control: Prevents chemical overuse and product waste, lowering operating
costs.
• Consistency: Guarantees uniform results across cleaning staff and shifts.
• Efficiency: Reduces training time and simpliﬁes the cleaning process.
By automating dilution, dispensers help protect workers, maintain compliance, and extend
the lifespan of cleaning equipment and surfaces.
Choosing the Right Dispenser
To achieve optimal performance, facilities should select dispensers that:
• Are designed for the speciﬁc chemical formulations being used.
• Can operate within the correct water pressure range (typically 40–70 psi).
• Are built with durable, chemical-resistant materials for longevity.
• Provide clear labeling and color coding to prevent cross-contamination.
Regular maintenance, calibration, and employee training are also essential to ensure
accurate dispensing and safe chemical handling.

Commercial Laundry vs. Residential Laundry
Laundry machines, whether in a household or commercial setting, follow similar
principles, but commercial machines are more complex, designed for higher volume and
efficiency. Timing, chemical use, and additional processing steps distinguish between the
two.
Residential Laundry Machines
Household laundry machines generally follow these steps:
1. Water Introduction: Water ﬁlls the drum to the required level.
2. Detergent Addition: Powder or liquid detergent is added directly to the wash.
3. Wash Cycle: Clothes are agitated to remove dirt and stains.
4. Rinse: Excess detergent is removed from fabrics.
5. Optional Bleach Addition: Added if required for stain removal or whitening.
6. Second Rinse: Ensures bleach is fully washed out.
7. Fabric Softener Addition: Softener is added for texture and fragrance.
8. Final Rinse: Ensures all chemicals are removed before spinning.
Commercial / Industrial Laundry Machines

Disinfectants
Disinfectants are essential in maintaining safe, hygienic environments by killing or
inactivating harmful microorganisms such as bacteria, viruses, and fungi. Understanding
the types of disinfectants—and how they work—is key to using them safely and effectively.
Different disinfectants have different modes of action, contact times, and surface
compatibilities. Always read the product label and Safety Data Sheet (SDS) before use.
Quaternary Ammonium Compounds (Quats)
Overview:
Quaternary disinfectants, also known as quats, are among the most commonly used
disinfectants in commercial cleaning. They work by disrupting the cell membranes of
microorganisms, leading to cell death.
How They Work:
Quats are positively charged molecules that are attracted to the negatively charged
surfaces of microbial cell membranes. This interaction weakens and breaks the
membrane, killing the microorganism.
Contact Time:
Quats typically require 60 seconds to 10 minutes of surface contact time to achieve
effective disinfection.
Common Examples:
• Betco Daily Disinfectant Plus
• Betco Daily Disinfectant Dual
• Certainty Wipes
• Clorox Disinfecting Wipes

Alcohol-Based Disinfectants
Overview:
Alcohols, such as ethyl or isopropyl alcohol, are used for rapid disinfection of non-porous
surfaces. They are ideal where quick drying and no residue are important, such as in
laboratories or on electronics.
How They Work:
Alcohols denature proteins and dissolve lipids, destroying microbial cells. However, they
are not effective against spores and require the surface to remain wet for several
minutes for proper disinfection.
Effective Concentration:
Best performance is achieved with 50–70% alcohol solutions.
Common Examples:
• Purell Wipes
Chlorine-Based Disinfectants
Overview:
Chlorine disinfectants use chlorine compounds to oxidize and destroy microorganisms.
They are highly effective against a wide range of pathogens, including viruses and bacteria.
How They Work:
Reactive chlorine species—especially hypochlorous acid (HOCl)—attack and oxidize cell
walls, proteins, and DNA, leading to microbial death.
Common Examples:
• Traditional Bleach
• Clorox Bleach Wipes
Note:
Chlorine disinfectants can be corrosive and produce strong fumes. Always use with proper
ventilation and never mix with ammonia or acids.

Detergents
Overview:
Detergents are primarily cleaning agents that remove dirt, oils, and organic material from
surfaces. While they are not high-level disinfectants, they are an important ﬁrst step
before disinfection.
How They Work:
Detergents (anionic, such as soap or sodium lauryl sulfate) suspend and rinse away soil
and microorganisms rather than killing them.
Key Tip:
Cleaning with a detergent before applying a disinfectant allows the disinfectant to contact
the surface more effectively.
Peroxide-Based Disinfectants
Overview:
Hydrogen peroxide is a versatile cleaner and disinfectant. While weak peroxide solutions
(like those used on minor wounds) have limited antimicrobial action, stabilized or
accelerated hydrogen peroxide (AHP) products offer rapid, powerful disinfection.
How They Work:
Peroxides destroy microorganisms through oxidation, breaking down their cell walls and
internal components.
Common Examples:
• Clorox Peroxide Wipes
• Clorox Peroxide Spray
• Virox (Accelerated Hydrogen Peroxide)
Phenolic Disinfectants
Overview:
Phenolics are effective disinfectants based on phenol compounds, which disrupt cell
walls and precipitate cellular proteins. They are commonly used for environmental surface
disinfection in healthcare and institutional settings.

How They Work:
Modern formulations use substituted phenolics, such as orthophenylphenol, for broad-
spectrum antimicrobial activity.
Dilution:
Typically diluted 1:128 to 1:256, depending on the application.
Common Examples:
• Lysol Disinfectant Products
Other Chemicals
Other substances—such as acetic acid, essential oils, carbonates, chlorites, and
dyes—have been used historically for antimicrobial purposes. However, these agents are
generally less effective than the disinfectants listed above and are not recommended for
professional cleaning programs.
Common Example:
• Green Earth Fight Bac
Important Notes for Safe Disinfection
• Always Clean Before Disinfecting: Soil and debris can reduce disinfectant
effectiveness.
• Follow Label Directions: Ensure correct dilution, application method, and
contact time.
• Wear PPE: Gloves, goggles, or masks may be required depending on the
product.
• Ensure Ventilation: Many disinfectants release fumes that require adequate
airﬂow.
• Never Mix Chemicals: Mixing can produce dangerous or toxic gases.

Effective Biological Application
Biological cleaning products use live microorganisms and enzymes to break down organic
matter that causes stains, odors, and residue. When used correctly, they are highly
effective, environmentally friendly, and long-lasting.
Biological agents thrive when all four conditions are present:
1. Moisture – The foundation of biological activity.
2. Food Source – The organic material you are trying to remove.
3. Suitable Environment – Proper temperature, limited disturbance, and surface
contact.
4. Time – 24–72 hours of active conditions for full remediation.
1. Identify the Odor Source
• Determine whether the issue is urine, vomit, feces, grease, food soil, or sewage
residue.
• Biologicals are most effective on organic-based contamination.
2. Select the Correct Product
• Read the product label to ensure it matches your cleaning task.
• Choose a formulation designed for the speciﬁc residue you are removing.
• Verify, the product is safe for the surface (carpet, drains, garbage bins, textiles,
septic systems).
3. Follow Label Directions Carefully
Proper dilution and application are essential:
• Dilution: Mix exactly as instructed for maximum biological activity.
• Drain & Trap Maintenance: Use 2 oz per inch of drain diameter daily.
• Septic Systems: Add 1 liter every 30 days for residential/small systems.
• Direct Surface Application: Apply directly to the affected area.
• General Odor Control: Use a 4:1 water-to-concentrate dilution unless
otherwise speciﬁed.

4. Create the Right Environment for Biological Activity
Biological products only work when the environment supports them:
Temperature
• Store and apply between 10–25°C for optimal microbial activity.
Time
• Biologicals need at least 24–72 hours of contact to work effectively.
Moisture
• Do not let treated surfaces dry too quickly.
• Reapply light moisture as needed for 36 hours when treating stains or stubborn
odors.
Chemical Compatibility
• Avoid using acidic, alkaline, or solvent cleaners before or after application.
• These chemicals can kill or disable biological organisms.
5. Repeat as Needed
• Do not rinse between treatments unless instructed.
• Reapply weekly for persistent odors.
• Daily maintenance may be required for drains, grease traps, and holding tanks.
Common Mistakes to Avoid
• Using incompatible chemicals before or after applying biologicals.
• Applying in freezing or extremely hot conditions.
• Expecting instant results—biological cleaning requires time.
• Allowing treated areas to dry too quickly.

Anti-Fatigue and Ergonomic Matting
Standing for long periods on hard, non-resilient ﬂoors can cause signiﬁcant discomfort and
fatigue. Whether in a factory, kitchen, or front-of-house setting, proper ergonomic matting
can make a remarkable difference in health, comfort, and productivity.
The Beneﬁts of Anti-Fatigue Matting
1. Reduced Discomfort
Anti-fatigue mats provide a cushioned surface that reduces pressure on the feet,
legs, and lower back. This helps relieve soreness and strain caused by long hours of
standing.
2. Improved Circulation
The mat’s ﬂexible surface encourages small, continuous leg and foot movements,
which promote better blood ﬂow and oxygen circulation—reducing the risk of
varicose veins and muscle fatigue.
3. Increased Productivity
By minimizing physical strain, employees experience less discomfort and can
maintain focus and energy for longer periods. Businesses often see a 10–25%
improvement in productivity when ergonomics are prioritized.
4. Enhanced Safety
Quality mats provide a non-slip surface, reducing the risk of slips and falls—
especially in areas where moisture or debris may be present.
5. Better Posture
Anti-fatigue mats help promote proper body alignment and posture by supporting
the natural balance and stance of the user.
6. Happier Workplaces
When employees feel more comfortable and supported, morale improves—
resulting in better service, teamwork, and customer satisfaction.

How Anti-Fatigue Matting Works
When standing for extended periods, blood ﬂow to the lower body is restricted, leading to
soreness and fatigue. Anti-fatigue mats work by providing a resilient, supportive surface
that slightly compresses underweight.
This causes subtle muscle movement in the legs and calves—stimulating blood ﬂow and
oxygen delivery to muscles.
Think of standing on a soft surface that gently “gives” under your weight—your body
instinctively adjusts, keeping blood circulating and muscles engaged.
Understanding Compression Deﬂection
Compression deﬂection measures how much a mat compresses under pressure,
determining its comfort and support level.
• A 20-psi load represents an average 150-pound person.
• A 40-psi load represents an average 600-pound weight.
For ideal comfort, deﬂection should range between 20% and 60%.
• Below 20% = too ﬁrm.
• Above 60% = too soft.
• Between 20–60% = “just right,” providing the best ergonomic balance.
Material and Performance Overview
The material composition of a mat directly affects its durability, comfort, and suitability for
speciﬁc environments.
PVC (Vinyl)
• Pros: Economical and lightweight.
• Cons: Less durable, prone to cracking, curling, and slipping when wet.
• Tip: If selecting vinyl, choose a molded (not glued) surface for improved
longevity and safety.
Rubber
• Types: Styrene-Butadiene Rubber (SBR) and Nitrile Rubber.
• Pros: Extremely slip-resistant, grease- and oil-resistant, and chemical-tolerant.

• Bonus: Naturally antimicrobial—ideal for hygiene-sensitive areas.
Polyurethane
• Pros: Excellent comfort, lightweight, and durable for light-to-moderate use.
• Cons: Not suitable for high-heat or industrial applications.

Selecting the correct mat for your environment ensures safety, comfort, and long-term
value.

Microﬁber Care and Use
Proper care of microﬁber cleaning cloths is essential to maintain their performance,
longevity, and hygienic quality. When handled correctly, microﬁber can last for hundreds of
wash cycles while continuing to deliver superior cleaning results.
Best Practices for Caring for Microﬁber Cloths
1. Wash Separately
Always wash microﬁber cloths separately from other laundry, especially cotton or
lint-producing fabrics. Lint can become trapped within the ﬁne ﬁbers, reducing the
cloth’s ability to attract and hold dust and debris.
2. Use a Mild Detergent
Choose a mild, liquid detergent free of fabric softeners, bleach, or fragrance
additives. These chemicals can coat or damage the microﬁber strands, reducing
their absorbency and cleaning power.
3. Avoid High Heat
Wash in warm or cold water only. When drying, use a low-heat setting or air dry.
Excessive heat can melt or distort the delicate synthetic ﬁbers, permanently
affecting their structure.
4. Do Not Iron
Never iron microﬁber cloths. The intense heat from an iron can cause the synthetic
ﬁbers to fuse together, rendering the cloth ineffective.
5. No Fabric Softeners or Dryer Sheets
Fabric softeners leave a waxy residue that clogs the microscopic pores in
microﬁber, preventing it from trapping dust and liquid effectively. Avoid using
softeners in both washing and drying cycles.
6. Avoid Bleach
Bleach degrades the synthetic ﬁbers, causing them to lose shape and performance.
Over time, it will break down the cloth entirely.
7. Rinse Thoroughly
After washing, ensure all detergent is completely rinsed out. Even mild soap residue
can diminish the ﬁber’s electrostatic cleaning ability.
8. Store Properly
Once clean and dry, store microﬁber cloths in a cool, dry, and dust-free location.
Avoid damp storage areas to prevent bacterial or mildew growth.

Performance and Longevity
When properly maintained, quality microﬁber cloths can be washed and reused 150–350
times before showing signiﬁcant wear. This not only improves performance and
sustainability but also signiﬁcantly reduces long-term cleaning costs.
To prevent cross-contamination, consider color-coding your microﬁber cloths by task —
for example, blue for general cleaning, red for restrooms, green for food areas, and yellow
for glass and mirrors.
Proper care ensures that microﬁber remains one of the most effective, economical, and
environmentally responsible tools in modern cleaning programs.

• Breaks soil loose from ﬂoor pores and grout lines.
• Removes residues that mopping cannot.

The pH Scale
The pH scale measures how acidic or basic a substance is, ranging from 0 to 14:
• 0–6.9: Acidic (e.g., lemon juice, vinegar)
• 7: Neutral (e.g., pure water)
• 7.1–14: Basic or alkaline (e.g., baking soda, bleach)
The pH scale is logarithmic. Each whole number change represents a tenfold increase or
decreases in acidity. For example, a solution with a pH of 4 is ten times more acidic than a
solution with a pH of 5.
Acids
Properties and Characteristics:
• pH Value: Less than 7; the lower the number, the stronger the acidity (e.g.,
hydrochloric acid can have a pH near 0).
• Hydrogen Ions (H⁺): Acids release hydrogen ions in water, often existing as
hydronium ions (H₃O⁺), which contribute to acidity.
• Taste: Typically sour (e.g., citric acid in lemons, acetic acid in vinegar).
• Reactivity with Metals: Many acids react with metals (like zinc or magnesium),
producing hydrogen gas and a salt property useful in metal cleaning or etching.
• Neutralization: Acids react with bases to produce water and a salt (e.g., HCl +
NaOH → H₂O + NaCl).
• Electrical Conductivity: Acidic solutions conduct electricity due to free ions,
making them electrolytes.
• Effect on Indicators: Acids turn blue litmus paper red, phenolphthalein
colorless, and methyl orange red.
• Corrosiveness: Strong acids (e.g., sulfuric acid, nitric acid) can damage metals,
organic materials, skin, and tissue.
Feel: Acids usually feel slightly abrasive or resistive on contact.

Alkalis (Bases)
Properties and Characteristics:
• pH Value: Greater than 7; higher numbers indicate stronger alkalinity (e.g.,
sodium hydroxide ≈ 13–14).
• Hydroxide Ions (OH⁻): Bases release hydroxide ions in water, which combine
with hydrogen ions to neutralize acids.
• Taste: Often bitter, though tasting chemicals is not recommended outside
controlled settings.
• Texture: Bases feel slippery or soapy due to reactions with fats and oils, forming
soap-like substances.
• Reactivity with Acids: Bases neutralize acids, producing water and a salt (e.g.,
NaOH + HCl → H₂O + NaCl).
• Electrical Conductivity: Aqueous solutions conduct electricity due to free ions.
• Effect on Indicators: Bases turn red litmus paper blue and can turn
phenolphthalein pink.
Feel: Alkaline solutions often feel slippery on the skin.

Summary
• Acids: pH < 7, sour, reactive with metals, corrosive, turn blue litmus red.
• Bases (Alkalis): pH > 7, bitter, slippery, neutralize acids, turn red litmus blue.
• Neutral: pH = 7, neither acidic nor basic (e.g., pure water).
Understanding the pH and properties of chemicals is critical for safe and effective
cleaning, maintenance, and chemical handling in both industrial and domestic
environments.
